subject: Cognitive Science
title: Bounded Rationality
description: Learn Bounded Rationality in one minute.

hook.text: You don't find the best restaurant in town. You pick the first decent one you see. That's rational enough.

buildup.text: Herbert Simon coined bounded rationality: humans don't optimize, they satisfice—find a good-enough option.

discovery.text: We're limited by time, information, and thinking capacity. Perfect decisions would take forever.

twist.text: Satisficing often outperforms optimizing. Perfectionists spend more time and get only marginally better results.

climax.text: Good decisions happen within constraints, not despite them. Shortcuts aren't flaws—they're designed features.

punchline.text: Good enough is often the best strategy.

quiz.question: What does 'satisficing' mean?
options: Choosing a good-enough option instead of the perfect one

details.summary: Herbert Simon proposed that humans are boundedly rational: we do not optimize decisions but satisfice, finding solutions that are good enough given our limited time, information, and cognitive capacity. Perfect rationality is impossible, so we use heuristics that work well most of the time.
details.whyItMatters: Bounded rationality reframes cognitive biases not as flaws but as adaptations to real-world constraints. It bridges economics and psychology.
takeaways: Human rationality is bounded by time, information, and cognition
We satisfice rather than optimize in most decisions
Heuristics are rational adaptations to bounded conditions

faq.question: What does satisficing mean?
faq.answer: Satisficing means choosing the first option that meets your minimum acceptable threshold rather than evaluating every possible option. You stop apartment hunting when you find one that is good enough.

faq.question: Is bounded rationality a weakness or a strength?
faq.answer: Both. It limits our ability to find optimal solutions, but the heuristics it produces often outperform complex optimization in uncertain, real-world environments. Simple rules that ignore most information frequently beat elaborate calculations when data is noisy and time is limited.
